VariantBench — Metabolic-Trait GWAS Follow-up (LDL_C, BCAA, Glucose, Lactate; EUR)

Khushi Goda

2026-07-26

1 Overview & method choices

Reproducibility. This document is the R Markdown source workflow/scripts/08_report.Rmd, knitted by the Snakemake report rule. Every number, table, and figure below is generated at knit time by reading the pipeline’s output files in results/ — nothing is hand-entered or pasted. Re-running the pipeline and re-knitting regenerates this report end to end, so the report cannot drift from the analysis it describes.

Scope of this knit. This version reports the completed steps: meta-analysis, LDSC, lead-variant definition, and fine-mapping + coding annotation (Steps 1–4), each followed by a multiple-choice question testing the biological reasoning behind that step. Steps 1–2 run across all four traits; Steps 3–4 are shown for LDL_C, the positive-control trait whose 11 canonical effector loci let the out-of-sample-LD behaviour be inspected locus by locus. Colocalization and Mendelian randomization (Steps 5–7) are in progress and will be folded into this same report — each with its own MCQ — once their pipeline rules have run.

This report follows four circulating metabolic traits — LDL cholesterol (LDL_C), total branched-chain amino acids (BCAA), glucose, and lactate — from published GWAS summary statistics through a standard post-GWAS causal-inference chain: cross-cohort meta-analysis, heritability and genetic correlation (LDSC), lead-variant definition, statistical fine-mapping, colocalization with gene expression, and Mendelian randomization against two cardiometabolic diseases. The analysis is European-ancestry throughout (EstBB + UKBB_EUR exposures, EUR-matched CAD/T2D outcomes, 1000G EUR LD reference), and no individual-level genotype data is used — every step operates on summary statistics plus a public LD reference.

The four exposures are chosen as a gradient of causal-prior strength, so the pipeline is shown to discriminate rather than merely run. LDL_C is the canonical positive control: the causal LDL→CAD relationship is proven by RCTs of statins (HMGCR), PCSK9 inhibitors (PCSK9), and ezetimibe (NPC1L1), so recovering a positive cis-MR at these drug-target genes is the strongest validation of the whole arc. BCAA (anchored by the catabolic regulators PPM1K / BCKDK) and glucose (anchored by GCK / GCKR / G6PC2 / SLC30A8) are further positive controls for the diabetes axis, both tested against T2D. Lactate is the contrast: different biology (glycolysis), a weaker causal prior, and a notable locus at GP6 (platelet collagen receptor) biologically distant from a metabolic-disease mechanism — a test of whether the methods correctly report a less compelling causal picture. Four exposures across four chromosomes and pathways demonstrate that the pipeline discriminates strong causal signals from weak ones.

Method choice stated up front — the LD reference is out-of-sample. Fine-mapping, clumping, and MR instrument pruning use a 1000 Genomes EUR panel, not the in-sample UKBB LD the reference paper used. Out-of-sample LD can miscalibrate SuSiE credible sets and mis-prune instruments; this is an accepted tractability tradeoff, flagged here and again in each affected section. A second deliberate choice concerns the CAD outcome: the paper’s Methods cite the multi-ancestry GCST90132315, but the authors’ released code uses the European-only GCST90132314. I use the European-only accession — it keeps exposure and outcome ancestry-matched and avoids a known source of two-sample MR bias, and it is the choice the authors’ own code made. (The multi-ancestry study is not used: with EUR-only exposures it would reintroduce the ancestry mismatch this design is built to avoid.) The CAD file is the GWAS Catalog harmonised (GRCh38) release, matching the GRCh38 metabolite exposures, so no CAD liftover is required; T2D (DIAGRAM, GRCh37) is lifted to GRCh38 in Step 0.

2 Meta-analysis (Step 1)

Inverse-variance fixed-effect meta-analysis of EstBB + UKBB (EUR), genome-wide (every union variant kept, not HapMap3-restricted). Validation: my meta effect sizes are regressed against the authors’ published meta-analysis — the OLS slope and Pearson r should both be ≈1 if the allele harmonization and inverse-variance weighting are correct.

The validation table is the decisive check on the whole meta step: pearson_r and slope at machine precision to 1 mean the from-scratch inverse-variance meta reproduces the authors’ published meta exactly, over all union variants. The overlap columns (n_both, n_estbb_only, n_ukbb_only) show that the meta genuinely combined both cohorts rather than defaulting to whichever one was present.

2.1 MCQ — Meta-analysis

A variant is genome-wide significant in the EstBB + UKBB meta-analysis but reached significance in neither cohort alone. The most appropriate interpretation is:

  • A. The meta-analysis has inflated type-I error, so the hit is probably false.
  • B. Increased sample size raised power; concordant same-direction effects combined to cross the threshold.
  • C. The variant must have opposite effects in the two cohorts.
  • D. It indicates a batch effect between cohorts.

Answer: B. Meta-analysis gains power precisely when per-cohort effects are concordant; a sub-threshold-but-consistent signal crossing genome-wide significance is the expected behaviour, not an artifact.

3 Heritability & genetic correlation (Step 2, LDSC)

SNP-heritability per (trait, dataset) and the paper’s two genetic-correlation analyses — A: rg between the three datasets (EstBB, UKBB_EUR, meta_EUR) for each trait; B: rg between the four traits within each dataset. The LDSC intercept is the key diagnostic: an intercept ≈1 means test-statistic inflation reflects polygenic signal, not population stratification or cryptic relatedness.

3.1 MCQ — Heritability (LDSC)

The LDSC regression for a trait returns an intercept ≈ 1.0. This indicates:

  • A. Severe population stratification inflating all test statistics.
  • B. Minimal confounding; inflation in the test statistics reflects genuine polygenic signal.
  • C. The heritability estimate is invalid.
  • D. Severe sample overlap between the two cohorts.

Answer: B. The LDSC intercept isolates confounding/inflation from polygenicity; an intercept near 1 means the elevated χ² comes from real polygenic signal, validating the h² estimate. (A markedly elevated intercept would instead flag stratification or sample overlap.)

4 Lead variants (Step 3)

Genome-wide-significant loci reduced to independent lead variants. Two design choices define this step:

1. Frequency-dependent significance. Common/low-frequency variants (MAF > 0.1%) use the standard genome-wide line P < 5e-8; rare variants (MAF < 0.1%) use a stricter Bonferroni line P < 0.05/8e7 = 6.25e-10, because the ~80M rare tests make 5e-8 anti-conservative. Variants whose effect-allele frequency is unknown fall back to the standard line and are flagged maf_class = "unknown" so the reader can weight them accordingly.

2. Distance-based locus definition. The most-significant unclaimed variant is taken as a lead, a 2 Mb locus (±1 Mb) is claimed around it, all variants inside are removed, and the process iterates. The brief’s Step 3 is summary-statistics-only and provides no genotype panel, so pairwise r² is not computable; the distance rule is the standard, honest substitute. The paper’s additional r²≥0.05 locus-merge (which stops an ultra-strong signal from “bleeding” past the 2 Mb window) and r²≥0.8 cross-trait clustering require a EUR genotype panel and are deferred to the LD-aware follow-on (Step 4 sourcing).

Concordance with the published loci. Benchmarked against the authors’ meta_EUR LDL_C lead variants, this step recovers 96.3% (310/322) of their loci at the exact lead position (321 leads called here vs 322 published). The small residual is expected under an out-of-sample 1000G-EUR LD reference: within a shared signal, a different reference can tag a slightly different sentinel SNP, so the locus is found but the precise lead variant occasionally differs.

4.1 MCQ — Lead variants

Step 3 calls lead variants with a frequency-dependent threshold: P < 5×10⁻⁸ for common variants (MAF > 0.1%) but the stricter P < 6.25×10⁻¹⁰ for rare variants. The rare-variant threshold is tightened because:

  • A. Rare variants have larger effect sizes, so they need a higher bar.
  • B. There are far more rare-variant tests (~80M), so the standard 5×10⁻⁸ line is anti-conservative and would admit too many false positives.
  • C. Rare variants are always artifacts and should be suppressed.
  • D. LDSC requires it for the heritability estimate.

Answer: B. The genome-wide 5×10⁻⁸ threshold is calibrated to ~1M independent common-variant tests. Adding ~80M rare-variant tests inflates the multiple-testing burden, so a Bonferroni-style tightening (0.05/8×10⁷) is needed to hold the family-wise error rate.

A follow-on on locus definition: this replication defines independent loci by distance (top SNP, then a ±1 Mb exclusion window, iterated) rather than by the paper’s LD-based r²≥0.05 merge. The main scientific limitation of the distance-only rule is:

  • A. It cannot handle more than one chromosome.
  • B. A single very strong signal (−log₁₀P ≫ 100) can generate association that extends beyond 2 Mb through LD, so distance clumping may split one true signal into several “independent” loci.
  • C. It systematically undercounts loci relative to LD clumping.
  • D. It requires an in-sample LD matrix to run.

Answer: B. LD can carry a strong association past a fixed window; the paper’s r²≥0.05 merge exists specifically to stop that “bleeding” and collapse the fragments into one locus. Distance clumping has no way to know two windows tag the same causal variant, so it can over-count. It is the honest choice only when no matched genotype panel is available to compute pairwise r² — which is the case here.

5 Fine-mapping + coding annotation (Step 4)

SuSiE fine-mapping per locus (MHC excluded), then missense/splice annotation of credible-set variants to nominate a candidate effector gene. Caveat: out-of-sample LD may miscalibrate credible sets — interpret set sizes and PIPs with that in mind.

Only the credible-set variants annotated as missense are shown below — these are the coding candidates that fine-mapping nominates as potentially causal. The recovery of textbook LDL coding variants (PCSK9 R46L, APOE C130R) at PIP = 1 is the strongest validation that the pipeline works despite the out-of-sample LD.

Three representative loci (of 11 fine-mapped). PCSK9 shows the R46L drug-target coding variant at high PIP; ABCG5/ABCG8 shows two missense variants across a two-gene locus; APOE shows a locus resolved into multiple credible sets. The remaining loci are summarised in the two figures above and available in the repository.

5.1 MCQ — Fine-mapping

The pipeline fine-maps with an out-of-sample 1000G EUR LD reference rather than the in-sample UKBB LD used by the reference paper. The primary risk this introduces to the credible sets is:

  • A. They will always be too small.
  • B. LD mismatch can miscalibrate posterior inclusion probabilities and yield spurious or oversized credible sets.
  • C. SuSiE cannot run at all without in-sample LD.
  • D. It only affects the Manhattan plot, not fine-mapping.

Answer: B. SuSiE-RSS assumes the LD matrix matches the GWAS sample; a mismatched reference distorts PIPs and credible-set membership. In this run the fingerprint is visible in the convergence QC (most loci hit the IBSS iteration cap), which is why an estimate_s_rss LD-mismatch diagnostic is reported per locus and estimate_residual_variance is fixed to FALSE — the documented remedy for out-of-sample LD. This is the single most important caveat of the analysis.

6 Limitations

  • Out-of-sample LD. Fine-mapping and distance-clumping use a 1000G EUR reference rather than in-sample LD; SuSiE credible sets may be miscalibrated (flagged per locus by the kriging diagnostic). This is the single most important caveat and the main methodological divergence from the reference paper, which had in-sample UKBB LD.
  • Distance-only locus definition. With no genotype panel provided at Step 3, independent loci are defined by a ±1 Mb distance rule rather than the paper’s r²≥0.05 LD merge; a very strong signal can bleed past the window and be split into apparent multiple loci (see the Step-3 MCQ).
  • Fine-mapping scoped to LDL effector loci. Step 4 fine-maps the 11 canonical LDL effector loci (a hypothesis-driven subset), not genome-wide — chosen so out-of-sample-LD behaviour can be inspected locus by locus.
  • Coding annotation explains few loci. Of the credible-set variants, only a handful are missense; most signal is regulatory/intronic. Resolving those mechanisms needs molecular-QTL colocalization — the next step, not yet included here.
  • EUR-only. Exposures and (planned) outcomes are European-ancestry, so estimates may not generalize — a deliberate choice to keep LD and allele frequencies matched.

Steps 5–7 (colocalization, Mendelian randomization) are in progress and will be added to this report, each with its own MCQ, once their pipeline rules have run.
